result:
There are 17 configurations. To see this, call two people "F-related" if they are friends or frenemies.

**Friendship classes.** The first rule says that friendship is transitive, so F-relatedness is an equivalence relation. Pairs in different classes are therefore enemies only. Pairs in the same class are friends or frenemies.

**Frenemies fill a whole class.** Suppose A and B are frenemies and C is in the same class.
- If B and C are friends, then A and B being enemies and B and C being friends forces A and C to be enemies. A and C are also F-related, so they are frenemies.
- If B and C are frenemies, then A and C are likewise frenemies by the same reasoning.

So a frenemy pair forces every pair in its class to be frenemies. Each class is therefore either all friends or all frenemies.

**At most two classes.** Take A, B, C in three different classes. Then A,B are enemies and B,C are enemies, so A and C must be friends. That contradicts them being in different classes. So there are at most 2 classes.

**Two classes exclude frenemies.** Suppose a class with at least 2 people is all frenemies and a second class exists. Take A, B in the first class and C in the second, so B and C are enemies. A,B frenemies and B,C enemies force A and C to contain both friend and enemy, so A and C must be frenemies. But A and C are in different classes, so they are only enemies. This is a contradiction. With two classes, every class of size at least 2 is therefore all friends.

**Counting.**
- One class: all friends or all frenemies, giving 2 configurations.
- Two classes: the number of ways to split 5 people into two nonempty unordered groups is 2⁴ − 1 = 15. Each split has a single valid assignment (all friends within groups, enemies between). Rules 2 and 3 check out for these.

Total: 2 + 15 = 17.

ANSWER: 17
